article.title: Justice for Nolan Wells
article.author: Melina Abdullah
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. It has been three months since Nolan Wells was murdered in Mississippi. Not drowned. Murdered. On Monday, Black Lives Matter – Los Angeles organizers met Nolan’s parents. I got to put my arms around his parents and pledge our continued support as they demand a federal investigation. Last week, our Georgia chapter, the BLM Youth Vanguard, and student organizers, mobilized thousands of Black college students at the Atlanta University Center. Nolan’s name has been spoken by activists, political officials, and celebrities. There has been news coverage. There was a social media blackout. Most know the story. On July 4th, the college football player joined a white friend-group for an outing to Horn Island. Nolan never returned. Two days later his body was discovered. Authorities quickly determined it a drowning. After immense public pressure, a grand jury was convened to affirm that determination, despite the two autopsies showed blunt force trauma to the back of Nolan’s head, no water in his airways, and deleted apps from his phone that had gone missing for hours after his disappearance. On September 21, the grand jury issued a “no bill” ruling and District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath quickly closed the case. Related: Old Is Not Ugly: Jasmine Guy and the Politics of Aging While Black There was a hung jury against Mississippi Capitol cop Michael Rhinewalt for the murder of Jaylen Lewis Jaylen was accused of a minor traffic violation. The Mississippi Attorney General is declining to retry the case. Rhinewalt shot a second Black man in the head (who survived) just a month later. He will stand trial for that later this month on “use of force” violation charges. On October 1st, Okaloosa County, Florida sheriff’s deputy Eddie Duran, who murdered the Senior Airman Roger Fortson, was found not guilty by a jury of all white men. Senior Airman Fortson was a celebrated, young, military man on active duty with the United States Airforce. On May 3, 2024, Roger was inside his own apartment, talking on the phone with his girlfriend. When Duran banged on his front door and shot Roger dead within seconds of him opening it. Okaloosa County Sheriffs say that Duran went to the wrong location. Hunter Foster, the white racist Senatobia, Mississippi cop who murdered 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot in June still hasn’t been charged with a crime. His chief at the time, Harold Vandeford, was fired in September for being caught sending anti-Black racist texts. A woman accompanying Baby Kohen’s mother had been accused of shoplifting a pack of diapers when Walmart called police on them. The cop shot the baby and the mother’s friend (who survived). Related: Congressional Black Caucus: When Black Excellence Is Not Black Power In Los Angeles, District Attorney Nathan Hochman still has not charged Brian Palacios, the ICE agent who murdered Black father, Keith Porter, on New Year’s Eve. Hochman dropped the charges against the Torrance police who killed Christopher DeAndre Mitchell and he has refused to file charges against Southern California Edison, which was determined responsible for causing the Altadena fires, which took the lives of 19 (mostly Black) people and destroyed 9419 structures in one of the most historic Black communities in the nation. This week in Erie, Pennsylvania, federal parole officer Kevin Seelinger will stand trial for the killing of Marchello Woodard last July. Black Lives Matter Grassroots Buffalo chapter organizers have been mobilizing alongside the family. Before the press event for Nolan Wells closed, we flyered the crowd, encouraging them to come to a rally in Nolan’s name on Wednesday. A mass march is planned for November 1st in Jackson, and an entire weekend of organizing November 21-23. These activations come after District Attorney McIlrath has already said “case closed.” They come with a demand that she reconsider and call for a federal investigation. Protests in front of Los Angeles’ Hall of (In)Justice are not just this Wednesday for Nolan Wells, but every Wednesday. Black Lives Matter Grassroots Florida continues to fight for Roger Fortson despite the “not guilty” verdict. Related: In the Name of Her Two Andrews, Deanna Joseph Carries the Fight Forward Some might say that these struggles are moot. That the call for justice in the names of Keith Porter and Baby Kohen Wiley are in vain. That organizing for Marchello Woodard is useless. Police and white-supremacy continue to murder Black people with impunity and the entire system is in cahoots. These are all true statements. And, to not fight, to resolve ourselves to the loss, is to betray each of the names we hashtag, our Ancestors, our divine calling, and our God. We muster the will to fight because we simply cannot accept the wholesale theft of our people’s lives. And it is more than just an exercise. Our fight, our resistance is not a pleading with a system that will never give us justice, or much of anything. Our fight is a simmering pot ready to boil over. And the system knows it. Our fight stands as a looming threat of impending revolution.
